facts.text: The white-naped honeyeater is native to eastern Australia and lives in dry eucalypt woodland.
facts.quote: is a passerine bird of the honeyeater family Meliphagidae native to eastern Australia.

facts.text: It is olive-green above and white below, with a black head, nape and throat and a red patch over the eye.
facts.quote: it is olive-green above and white below, with a black head, nape and throat, a red patch over the eye, and a white crescent-shaped patch on the nape.

facts.text: A white crescent on its nape gives the species its name, referring to the Latin luna, meaning 'moon'.
facts.quote: The specific epithet is derived from the Latin luna, meaning 'moon'; this refers to the crescent-shaped, white marking on its nape.

facts.text: It feeds mainly on nectar from a variety of flowers, supplemented by insects and other invertebrates.
facts.quote: Its diet is principally nectar from a variety of flowers, supplemented by insects and various other invertebrates.

facts.text: It nests from July to December and may breed once or twice during that period.
facts.quote: White-naped honeyeaters may nest from July to December, breeding once or twice during this time.

facts.text: The nest is a thick-walled bowl of grasses and bits of bark, built in the fork of a tall tree, usually a eucalypt.
facts.quote: The nest is a thick-walled bowl of grasses and bits of bark in the fork of a tall tree, usually a eucalypt.

facts.text: Females lay two or three shiny, buff-pink eggs sparsely spotted with red-brown.
facts.quote: Two or three eggs are laid, 18 mm × 14 mm (0.71 in × 0.55 in) in size, and shiny, buff-pink, sparsely spotted with red-brown.

facts.text: Young birds can be told by their brownish crowns and orange base of the bill.
facts.quote: Juveniles have brownish crowns and an orange base of  the bill.
